summary: This experimental memo proposes short-term solutions for keeping and distributing routing information for X.400 message handling, and shows how messages can travel over different networks using multi-stack relays.

plainLanguage.summary: Email in a different system needs directions about where to send it next. This paper suggests a table of directions and relay stops for X.400 mail.

subtitle: A table-based format for coordinating X.400 mail routing across multiple networks and stacks.

tldr.problem: X.400 MHS systems need a standard way to share routing information when multiple organizations operate separate X.400 domains that must interoperate over different network technologies and protocol stacks.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 1465 defines four document types (Community, Relay-MTA, Domain, and Person documents) that describe MHS communities, the MTAs that relay between them, the address subtrees served, and contact information. This allows coordinated routing until X.500 directory services become widely available.
tldr.outcome: This table format V3 has been used in the COSINE-MHS research network and other communities to manage routing for hundreds of X.400 MTAs across continents, serving as a bridge technology toward directory-based routing.

today: RFC 1465 is an Experimental protocol that served as a crucial bridge technology for X.400 routing during the 1990s. It has been superseded by X.500 directory services and eventually by the decline of X.400 in favor of Internet SMTP, but it remains a well-documented example of coordination protocols for multi-network environments.

sections.title: X.400 Routing Problems and the Need for Coordination
sections.content:
By 1993, X.400 message handling was growing rapidly, especially in commercial and research environments. Unlike Internet SMTP/TCP/IP systems that had automatic routing via DNS lookups, X.400 MTAs had no directory service and routing remained table-based. Additionally, unlike SMTP which had a single standard protocol stack, X.400 systems supported multiple transport and network stacks: TP0 over X.25, TP4 over CLNS, RFC1006 over TCP/IP, and TP0 over CONS.

Two fundamental problems emerged: first, where should new X.400 addresses be routed? Second, how could an MTA connect to another MTA's domain when they did not share the same underlying network technology? RFC 1465 proposes a solution: a standardized set of documents describing the structure and routing rules for an MHS community of interconnected domains.
sections.plainLanguage: Different X.400 systems spoke different network languages and had no shared address book. The RFC created a rulebook so they could coordinate.

sections.title: The Four Document Types and MHS Structure
sections.content:
RFC 1465 defines four types of documents for an MHS community. The Community document describes the overall community, lists the mandatory and optional service types (network/stack combinations) that members must support, and provides the contact information and file server addresses for the coordination point. Relay-MTA documents describe each RELAY-MTA (the RFC's term for a message transfer agent serving as a relay point). Each Relay-MTA document lists all the networks and stacks it supports, its addresses on those networks, and the technical details for connecting to it.

The Domain document describes an MHS domain (a group of mailboxes under the same administrative control) and lists which Relay-MTAs serve that domain, prioritized so that failing MTAs can be retried in order. The Person document contains contact information for administrators and responsible persons referenced in other documents. These documents are designed for both human readability and automated processing by configuration tools.
sections.plainLanguage: Community describes the group. Relay-MTA describes each helper. Domain describes where the mailboxes are and who helps them. Person lists phone numbers.

sections.title: Multi-Stack Relays and Protocol Bridges
sections.content:
A key innovation in this RFC is the multi-stack relay model. When two MHS domains cannot directly communicate because they support different network stacks, a Relay-MTA that supports both stacks can relay messages between them. For example, an organization using only X.25 can have its mail relayed through a Relay-MTA that supports both X.25 and TCP/IP, allowing it to reach organizations on the Internet.

The RFC distinguishes between primary and secondary Relay-MTAs. Primary Relay-MTAs must support all mandatory services in the community and must be able to connect to all other primary Relay-MTAs. Secondary Relay-MTAs need only connect to at least one primary Relay-MTA. This structure allows new MTAs to join as secondary while being tested, then be promoted to primary status when reliable.
sections.plainLanguage: A relay server that speaks both languages can carry mail from an X.25 system to a TCP/IP system.

sections.title: Routing Rules and Priority Schemes
sections.content:
When an MTA needs to route a message to an address in another domain, it uses a seven-step algorithm defined in section 6 of the RFC. First, it finds the Domain document entry that matches the recipient address. Second, it filters the list of Relay-MTAs to only those that have at least one service type in common with itself. Third, it removes secondary Relay-MTAs if direct connections are not desired. Fourth, it selects the Relay-MTA with the highest priority (lowest number).

If the selected Relay-MTA has specific service-type priorities configured, the MTA uses those to choose which network to try first. If that network fails, it tries the next preferred service type. If the selected Relay-MTA is unreachable, the MTA may try other Relay-MTAs with the same or lower priority. The RFC defines priority ranges 0-49 for backup Relay-MTAs and 50-99 for optional relays, allowing load sharing and graceful degradation.
sections.plainLanguage: Try the best relay first. If it fails, try the next best. Different relays can be tried for different network types to spread the load.

sections.title: Coordination Point and Operational Requirements
sections.content:
Each MHS community needs an identified coordination point responsible for registering new members, testing Relay-MTAs, assisting new domains with setup, and maintaining an up-to-date file server with all documents. The RFC recommends this file server be reachable via email, with optional FTP and FTAM access for automated tool support. Documents include version information and validity dates, allowing controlled rollout of updates.

The RFC notes that about 60 Relay-MTAs per community is the practical limit without automated tools and X.500 directory support. With 35 Relay-MTAs already in the COSINE-MHS service at the time of publication, the authors acknowledged that a core backbone of well-operated super-Relay-MTAs would eventually be needed.
sections.plainLanguage: One organization coordinates everything, keeps the address book updated, and tests new relay servers.

references.text: Eppenberger, U., et al., "Routing Coordination for X.400 MHS Services", RFC 1465, May 1993.
